blocks.title: Radiant flux intensity
blocks.text: Radiant flux intensity, F, is the amount of electromagnetic energy per unit area per unit time from a star that reaches the Earth's surface (or any point at a distance d from the star). It is a small fraction of the total luminosity.

For a star at a distance d, the radiant flux intensity is F = L / (4 pi d^2) (21.2), where L is the luminosity. As the luminosity of a star is constant, the radiant flux intensity follows an inverse-square law with distance (Fig 21.1): when the distance from the star is doubled (from r to 2r), the intensity falls to one-quarter; at three times the distance it falls by a factor of nine, and so on.

blocks.alt: A point source on the left with straight lines spreading from it. At distance r the lines pass the edges of one square; at 2r the same lines enclose a square made of four such squares; at 3r a square of nine squares. Marks below show the distances r, 2r and 3r from the source.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.1: Schematic illustration of the inverse-square law for radiant flux intensity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.1).

blocks.text: The luminosity of a star is 4.50 x 10^26 W. It is 1.40 x 10^11 m from a planet. Calculate the radiant flux intensity at the planet's surface. Solution: F = L / (4 pi r^2) = 4.50 x 10^26 W / (4 x 3.14 x (1.40 x 10^11 m)^2) = 1.83 x 10^3 W m^-2.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: If Earth were twice as far from the Sun, the sunlight reaching it would be only one-quarter as intense; such low energy might have made the evolution of life impossible.
Two stars appear equally bright in the night sky, but one is 10 times farther away than the other. Which is more luminous, and by how much?
